'''Russell Eugene Washington''' (December 17, 1946 – August 5, 2021)<ref name="stats"/> was an American professional [[American football|football]] [[Tackle (gridiron football position)|offensive tackle]] who played for the [[San Diego Chargers]] of the [[American Football League]] (AFL) and [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1968 to 1982, playing his first two seasons as a [[defensive tackle]]. He was selected in the first round of the [[1968 NFL/AFL draft]] with the fourth overall pick. He played [[college football]] for the [[Missouri Tigers football|Missouri Tigers]].

Washington was noted for his size (6 foot 6 inches, close to 300 pounds) and durability. A [[List of NFL players who spent their entire career with one franchise|one-team player]], he played in 200 games for the Chargers, including a 148-game streak as their starting right tackle that lasted over a decade. A strong player on a weak team throughout much of his career, his only playoff appearances came in his last four seasons. During this time he was part of an experienced [[Lineman (gridiron football)#Offensive line|offensive line]] that played a key role in the record-breaking [[Air Coryell]] passing attack.

'''Russell Davis III''' (born September 15, 1956) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player.

He played in the 1979 [[East–West Shrine Game]] and set Shrine Game records with six touchdowns and 199 rushing yards.

Davis played as a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] from 1979 to 1983. He appeared in 42 games for the Steelers, only two as a starter, and totaled 472 rushing yards, 168 yards on kickoff returns, and 45 receiving yards.

'''Russell Carrington Wilson''' (born November 29, 1988) is an American sportscaster and former professional [[American football|football]] [[quarterback]] who played for 14 seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL), primarily with the [[Seattle Seahawks]]. With the Seahawks, Wilson was named to the [[Pro Bowl]] nine times and helped Seattle win their first [[Super Bowl]] championship in [[Super Bowl XLVIII]]. He is regarded as one of the greatest [[dual-threat quarterback]]s of all time.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lee |first=Nick |date=November 5, 2020 |title=It's Time to Acknowledge Russell Wilson as Greatest Dual-Threat Quarterback in NFL History |url=https://www.si.com/nfl/seahawks/news/its-time-to-acknowledge-russell-wilson-as-greatest-dual-threat-quarterback-in-nfl-history/ |access-date=January 6, 2022 |website=SI.com}}</ref> He is also a former professional baseball player.

Wilson played both [[college football]] and baseball for the [[NC State Wolfpack football|NC State Wolfpack]] from 2008 to 2010 before transferring to the [[Wisconsin Badgers football|Wisconsin Badgers]] in 2011, where he set the single-season [[Football Bowl Subdivision|FBS]] record for passer rating and led them to a [[2011 Big Ten Football Championship Game|Big Ten title]] and the [[2012 Rose Bowl]]. He also played [[Minor League Baseball|minor league]] baseball for the [[Tri-City Dust Devils]] in 2010 and the [[Asheville Tourists]] in 2011 as a [[second baseman]]. The Seattle Seahawks selected Wilson in the third round (75th overall) of the [[2012 NFL draft]]. He tied the rookie record for most passing touchdowns and was named [[Pepsi NFL Rookie of the Year]].<ref name="pepsiroy">{{Cite web |date=March 29, 2013 |title=Russell Wilson named 2012 NFL Rookie of the Year |url=http://www.seahawks.com/news/articles/article-1/Russell-Wilson-named-2012-NFL-Rookie-of-the-Year/08c16850-7f38-4792-8942-dff72c75c662 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130206083407/http://www.seahawks.com/news/articles/article-1/Russell-Wilson-named-2012-NFL-Rookie-of-the-Year/08c16850-7f38-4792-8942-dff72c75c662 |archive-date=February 6, 2013 |access-date=April 3, 2013 |website=Seahawks.com}}</ref> Wilson led the Seahawks to consecutive Super Bowl appearances over the next two seasons, winning Super Bowl XLVIII and losing [[Super Bowl XLIX]] after he was intercepted at the goal line by [[Malcolm Butler]].  He led the team to eight total playoff appearances with four division titles.

Wilson holds the record for most wins by an NFL quarterback through nine seasons and is one of five quarterbacks with a [[NFL career passer rating leaders|career passer rating]] over 99.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Warner |first=Jonathan |date=November 19, 2020 |title=Russell Wilson becomes NFL's all-time winningest quarterback through 9 seasons |url=https://www.nbcsports.com/northwest/seahawks/russell-wilson-becomes-nfls-all-time-winningest-quarterback-through-9-seasons |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220814194530/https://www.nbcsports.com/northwest/seahawks/russell-wilson-becomes-nfls-all-time-winningest-quarterback-through-9-seasons |archive-date=August 14, 2022 |access-date=June 19, 2022 |website=NBC Sports – Northwest}}</ref> In 2019, he signed a four-year, $140 million contract extension with the Seahawks, becoming the highest-paid NFL player at the time. In 2020, he became the third quarterback in NFL history to throw 30 touchdowns in four consecutive seasons.<ref name="TD Feat">{{Cite web |last=Sullivan |first=Tyler |date=November 20, 2020 |title=Russell Wilson joins Brett Favre and Drew Brees as only three quarterbacks to accomplish rare feat |url=https://www.cbssports.com/nfl/news/russell-wilson-joins-brett-favre-and-drew-brees-as-only-three-quarterbacks-to-accomplish-rare-feat/ |access-date=November 30, 2020 |website=CBSSports.com}}</ref> Wilson was traded to the Broncos in 2022 and later signed a five-year, $245 million extension. His time with the Broncos was largely unsuccessful, with the Broncos having the league's worst scoring offense in 2022. Wilson was benched near the end of the 2023 season and was released in the offseason, later signing a one-year deal with the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] for 2024 where he earned his tenth Pro Bowl selection. The next season he signed a one-year contract with the New York Giants. In 2026, he retired from the NFL to join [[CBS Sports]] as a sportscaster.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Baca |first=Michael  |date=June 1, 2026 |title=NFL Network: Russell Wilson accepts offer to join CBS Sports, putting pause on playing career |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/russell-wilson-cbs-sports-putting-pause-on-playing-career |access-date=2026-06-02 |website=NFL.com |language=en-US}}</ref> He retired as the only quarterback with both 40,000 passing yards and 5,000 rushing yards.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/stathead/tiny/x22Rq|access-date=June 5, 2026|website=Stathead|title=For combined seasons, in the regular season, requiring Passing Yds >= 40000 and Rushing Yds >= 5000, sorted by descending Passing Yds.}}</ref>

Noted for his philanthropy, Wilson was named the [[Walter Payton NFL Man of the Year award|Walter Payton Man of the Year]] in 2020 and was the recipient of the [[Bart Starr Award]] in 2022. Wilson is also part owner of the [[Seattle Sounders FC]] of [[Major League Soccer]] (MLS). After he purchased his minority stake, the Sounders won [[MLS Cup 2019]] and the [[2022 CONCACAF Champions League]].
